_meta.description: REST API vulnerability knowledge base for APISec scanner.

CORS-001.label: Reflected Origin CORS Misconfiguration
CORS-001.impact: Any malicious website can read this API's responses on behalf of an authenticated victim.
CORS-001.description: The server reflects the attacker-controlled Origin header without validation. Any malicious website can send cross-origin requests to this API and read the response on behalf of an authenticated victim.
CORS-001.solution: Maintain an explicit server-side allowlist of trusted origins. Validate the Origin header against this allowlist before reflecting it. Never reflect arbitrary origins.

CORS-002.label: Wildcard CORS with Credentials Enabled
CORS-002.impact: Complete authentication bypass — attacker receives victim's authenticated session cookies and tokens.
CORS-002.description: The API sets both Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. This combination is explicitly forbidden by the CORS specification and allows any origin to make credentialed cross-origin requests.
CORS-002.solution: Never combine wildcard CORS with credentials. Use a strict origin allowlist if credentials are required.

CORS-003.label: Unrestricted Wildcard CORS Origin
CORS-003.impact: Any website can read this API's responses — data exfiltration risk.
CORS-003.description: The API allows cross-origin requests from any domain via a wildcard Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. Any website can read this API's responses.
CORS-003.solution: Restrict CORS to an explicit allowlist of trusted origins.

HDR-001.label: Missing Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS)
HDR-001.impact: Browsers may connect over plain HTTP, exposing credentials and tokens to network interception.
HDR-001.description: The Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) header is absent. Without HSTS, browsers may connect to the API over plain HTTP, exposing credentials and session tokens to network-level interception (man-in-the-middle attacks).

HDR-002.label: Missing X-Content-Type-Options
HDR-002.impact: Browsers may MIME-sniff responses, potentially executing malicious scripts.
HDR-002.description: The X-Content-Type-Options header is absent. Without it, browsers may MIME-sniff responses away from the declared content type, potentially executing malicious scripts disguised as benign content.

HDR-003.label: Missing X-Frame-Options
HDR-003.impact: Clickjacking attacks — users tricked into performing unintended actions.
HDR-003.description: The X-Frame-Options header is absent. This allows the API responses to be embedded in iframes on third-party pages, enabling clickjacking attacks where users are tricked into performing unintended actions.
HDR-003.solution: Add: X-Frame-Options: DENY (or SAMEORIGIN if framing is needed internally)

HDR-004.label: Missing Content-Security-Policy (CSP)
HDR-004.impact: No defense against XSS — malicious scripts can be injected and executed.
HDR-004.description: The Content-Security-Policy header is absent. CSP is a critical defense against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks by specifying which sources of content are allowed to be loaded and executed by the browser.
HDR-004.solution: Define a strict CSP policy. Minimum: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'

INFO-001.label: Server Version Disclosure
INFO-001.impact: Attacker can identify known CVEs for the specific server version.
INFO-001.description: The Server header exposes the web server software name and version. This information allows attackers to identify known CVEs targeting the specific version and craft targeted exploits.
INFO-001.solution: Configure the server to return a generic value (e.g. Server: webserver) or suppress the header entirely.

INFO-002.label: Technology Stack Disclosure via X-Powered-By
INFO-002.description: The X-Powered-By header reveals the backend technology and version (e.g. PHP/7.2.1, ASP.NET). This fingerprinting information aids attackers in identifying framework-specific vulnerabilities.
INFO-002.solution: Remove the X-Powered-By header. In Express.js: app.disable('x-powered-by'). In PHP: expose_php = Off.

VERB-001.label: HTTP TRACE Method Enabled
VERB-001.impact: XST attacks — HttpOnly cookies and Authorization headers exposed via reflected request.
VERB-001.description: The HTTP TRACE method is enabled. It reflects the full request back, enabling Cross-Site Tracing (XST) attacks that can expose HttpOnly cookies and Authorization headers.
VERB-001.solution: Apache: TraceEnable Off. Nginx: if ($request_method = TRACE) { return 405; }.

ERR-001.label: Verbose Error / Stack Trace Exposure
ERR-001.impact: Internal details (stack traces, file paths, DB queries, framework versions) aid attacker reconnaissance.
ERR-001.description: The API returns verbose error messages containing stack traces, internal file paths, database error strings, or framework version information. This information is valuable for attackers profiling the backend stack.
ERR-001.solution: Return generic error messages in production. Log detailed errors server-side only. Use error masking middleware.

AUTH-001.label: Endpoint Accessible Without Authentication Token
AUTH-001.impact: Protected resources accessible to unauthenticated users.
AUTH-001.description: This endpoint returns data without any authentication token. Protected resources are accessible to unauthenticated users.
AUTH-001.solution: Enforce authentication middleware on every protected route. Validate the token before any business logic executes.

AUTH-002.label: Endpoint Accepts Invalid / Forged Token
AUTH-002.impact: Token signature, structure, and content are not validated — trivial authentication bypass.
AUTH-002.description: The server returns 200 with a completely invalid token. Token signature, structure, and content are not validated.
AUTH-002.solution: Validate token signature, expiry, issuer, and audience on every request. Return 401 for any token that fails validation.

AUTH-003.label: JWT 'none' Algorithm Accepted
AUTH-003.impact: Complete authentication bypass — any attacker can forge arbitrary tokens without a secret key.
AUTH-003.description: The server accepted a JWT with alg:none — no cryptographic signature. Any attacker can forge arbitrary tokens without knowing any secret key. This is a complete authentication bypass.
AUTH-003.solution: Explicitly reject alg:none. Hardcode the expected algorithm server-side. Never trust the algorithm from the token header.

AUTH-004.label: JWT Algorithm Confusion (RS256 -> HS256)
AUTH-004.impact: Attacker can forge any token without knowing the private key.
AUTH-004.description: Server accepted a token where the algorithm was changed from RS256 to HS256, signed with the public RSA key as HMAC secret. Attacker can forge any token without knowing the private key.
AUTH-004.solution: Hardcode the expected algorithm server-side. Use: jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=['RS256']). Never read the algorithm from the token header.

AUTH-005.label: No Rate Limiting on Login Endpoint
AUTH-005.impact: Unlimited brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks possible.
AUTH-005.description: The login endpoint does not enforce any rate limiting. An attacker can send unlimited authentication attempts without being blocked or slowed down, enabling brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks.
AUTH-005.solution: Return HTTP 429 after N failed attempts. Add Retry-After, X-RateLimit-* headers. Consider account lockout and CAPTCHA for suspicious IPs.

SQLI-001.label: SQL Injection
SQLI-001.owasp: API3:2023 - Broken Object Property Level Authorization
SQLI-001.impact: Full database compromise — data exfiltration, authentication bypass, RCE.
SQLI-001.description: SQL injection detected. User-supplied input is incorporated into SQL queries without parameterization, allowing an attacker to manipulate the query logic.
SQLI-001.solution: Use parameterized queries or prepared statements exclusively. Never interpolate user input directly into SQL strings.

MASS-001.label: Mass Assignment — Hidden Field Injection
MASS-001.owasp: API3:2023 - Broken Object Property Level Authorization
MASS-001.impact: Privilege escalation, financial manipulation, account takeover via hidden model fields.
MASS-001.description: A hidden model field was accepted and applied by the server via a POST/PUT/PATCH request. The server uses a mass assignment pattern (e.g. User(**request.json)) that binds all request fields to the model without filtering, allowing attackers to modify fields not intended to be user-writable.
MASS-001.solution: Use an explicit allowlist (DTO pattern) — only bind fields that users are permitted to modify. Never use wildcard binding from request bodies.

INV-001.label: Exposed API Documentation
INV-001.impact: Full API surface exposed to attackers — all endpoints, parameters, and auth schemes revealed.
INV-001.description: A Swagger/OpenAPI specification or API documentation interface is publicly accessible. This reveals the complete API surface to attackers, including undocumented endpoints, parameter names, authentication schemes, and data models.
INV-001.solution: Restrict access to API documentation in production. Use authentication or IP allowlisting. Consider disabling Swagger UI entirely in production environments.

INV-002.label: Sensitive File Exposed
INV-002.impact: Credentials, API keys, database connection strings, or infrastructure details exposed.
INV-002.description: A sensitive file (.env, config, backup, source control metadata) is publicly accessible via HTTP. These files may contain credentials, API keys, database passwords, private keys, or infrastructure architecture details that enable further compromise.
INV-002.solution: Remove sensitive files from web-accessible directories. Configure the web server to deny access to .env, .git, .bak, and config files. Use web server rules to block these patterns.

INV-003.label: Debug or Admin Endpoint Exposed
INV-003.impact: Internal application state, environment variables, heap dumps, or admin functionality exposed.
INV-003.description: A debug or administrative endpoint is publicly accessible. These endpoints expose internal application state (environment variables, bean definitions, request mappings, heap dumps) or provide administrative functionality that should not be accessible in production.
INV-003.solution: Disable or restrict debug endpoints in production. For Spring Boot Actuator: configure management.endpoints.web.exposure.include with only safe endpoints. Apply authentication to all admin interfaces.

INV-004.label: Deprecated API Version Active
INV-004.impact: Old API versions may lack security patches, rate limiting, and authentication improvements.
INV-004.description: A deprecated API version is still active alongside the current version. Old API versions frequently lack security patches, input validation improvements, rate limiting, and authentication hardening applied to newer versions. Attackers deliberately target old versions to bypass security controls.
INV-004.solution: Decommission deprecated API versions. Implement a versioning lifecycle policy. If old versions must remain, ensure full security parity with the current version.

SENS-001.label: Plaintext Password Exposed in API Response
SENS-001.owasp: API3:2023 - Broken Object Property Level Authorization
SENS-001.impact: Plaintext user credentials exposed — immediate account takeover risk.
SENS-001.description: The API response contains a 'password' or equivalent field with a non-empty plaintext value. Passwords must never be returned in API responses, even in internal or administrative endpoints.
SENS-001.solution: Exclude all password fields from API serializers and response DTOs. Apply a response filter layer that strips credential fields before serialization.

SENS-002.label: Client Secret / Application Secret Exposed in Response
SENS-002.owasp: API3:2023 - Broken Object Property Level Authorization
SENS-002.impact: OAuth client secrets or signing secrets exposed — enables token forgery and full API impersonation.
SENS-002.description: The API response contains a 'secret', 'client_secret', or equivalent field with a non-empty value. Secrets are used to sign tokens and authenticate services — their exposure allows complete impersonation of the application.
SENS-002.solution: Never return secret fields in API responses. Store secrets server-side only. Use write-only semantics for sensitive configuration fields.

SENS-003.label: API Key / Access Key Exposed in Response Body
SENS-003.owasp: API3:2023 - Broken Object Property Level Authorization
SENS-003.impact: Third-party service credentials exposed — enables unauthorized API calls billed to the victim.
SENS-003.description: The API response contains an 'api_key', 'access_key', or equivalent field with a non-empty value. Exposed API keys allow attackers to make authenticated calls to third-party services (payment processors, cloud providers, messaging platforms) under the victim's account.
SENS-003.solution: Remove API key fields from all response serializers. Use write-only fields or separate key management endpoints with strict access control.

SENS-004.label: Private Key Material Exposed in Response Body
SENS-004.owasp: API3:2023 - Broken Object Property Level Authorization
SENS-004.impact: RSA/EC/SSH private key exposed — enables decryption of historical traffic and complete identity impersonation.
SENS-004.description: The API response contains a field named 'private_key', 'rsa_key', or equivalent with a non-empty value. Exposed private keys allow attackers to decrypt previously captured TLS traffic, forge authentication tokens, and fully impersonate the server or user.
SENS-004.solution: Private keys must never be stored in or returned by application databases or APIs. Use hardware security modules (HSMs) or secrets managers (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager).

SENS-005.label: Government Identity Number (SSN/NID) Exposed in Response
SENS-005.owasp: API3:2023 - Broken Object Property Level Authorization
SENS-005.impact: Social security or national identity numbers exposed — enables identity theft and regulatory violations (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS).
SENS-005.description: The API response contains a field named 'ssn', 'nid', 'national_id', or equivalent. Government-issued identity numbers are classified as Personally Identifiable Information (PII) and their exposure triggers regulatory obligations and identity theft risk.
SENS-005.solution: Mask or exclude identity numbers from API responses. Return only the last 4 digits if display is required. Enforce field-level access control — only privileged roles should access full identity numbers.

SENS-006.label: Payment Card Data Exposed in Response Body
SENS-006.owasp: API3:2023 - Broken Object Property Level Authorization
SENS-006.impact: Full payment card data exposed — PCI-DSS violation, financial fraud enablement.
SENS-006.description: The API response contains a field named 'credit_card', 'card_number', 'cvv', 'pan', or equivalent. Returning full card data violates PCI-DSS requirements and exposes users to financial fraud. CVV codes must never be stored or returned after transaction authorization.
SENS-006.solution: Never return full card numbers or CVV codes in API responses. Use tokenization (Stripe, Braintree) and return only masked card representations (e.g. **** **** **** 4242).

SENS-007.label: AWS Access Key ID Exposed in Response
SENS-007.impact: AWS infrastructure access — S3 buckets, EC2 instances, IAM roles, and all attached permissions accessible to attacker.
SENS-007.description: An AWS Access Key ID (pattern: AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}) was detected in the API response. AWS credentials embedded in API responses expose cloud infrastructure to unauthorized access, data exfiltration, and resource abuse.
SENS-007.solution: Rotate the exposed AWS key immediately. Remove credentials from application code and API responses. Use IAM roles and instance profiles instead of static access keys.

SENS-008.label: Potential AWS Secret Access Key Exposed in Response
SENS-008.impact: If confirmed, AWS infrastructure fully compromised.
SENS-008.description: A 40-character alphanumeric string matching the AWS Secret Access Key format was detected. This detection has LOW confidence — manual verification is required to confirm it is a real AWS secret key rather than another type of encoded value.
SENS-008.solution: If confirmed: rotate the key immediately, audit CloudTrail for unauthorized usage, and remove the credential from the response.

SENS-009.label: Stripe Live Secret Key Exposed in Response
SENS-009.impact: Full Stripe account access — charges, refunds, customer data, and payout manipulation.
SENS-009.description: A Stripe live secret key (sk_live_...) was detected in the API response. This key grants full access to the Stripe account including the ability to create charges, issue refunds, access customer payment methods, and modify payout settings.
SENS-009.solution: Rotate the Stripe key immediately via the Stripe dashboard. Never return payment processor credentials in API responses. Use restricted keys with minimal required permissions.

SENS-010.label: Twilio Account SID / Auth Token Exposed in Response
SENS-010.impact: Full Twilio account access — SMS/voice abuse, phone number hijacking, billing fraud.
SENS-010.description: A Twilio Account SID or Auth Token (pattern: SK[0-9a-fA-F]{32}) was detected in the API response. These credentials grant full access to the Twilio account including sending SMS, making calls, and purchasing phone numbers at the account owner's expense.
SENS-010.solution: Rotate Twilio credentials immediately. Use API Keys instead of Auth Tokens for application authentication. Never expose communication platform credentials in API responses.

SENS-011.label: JWT Token Exposed in Response Body
SENS-011.owasp: API3:2023 - Broken Object Property Level Authorization
SENS-011.impact: Session hijacking — attacker can authenticate as the token's subject for its remaining validity period.
SENS-011.description: A JWT token (eyJ...) was detected in the API response body outside of its expected login response context. JWTs found in data endpoints (profile, orders, users) indicate tokens are being stored and returned as data, creating a session hijacking risk.
SENS-011.solution: JWTs should only be returned in authentication responses (login, token refresh). Never store or return tokens as data fields in resource endpoints.

SENS-012.label: PEM Private Key Block Exposed in Response
SENS-012.impact: RSA/EC/SSH private key fully exposed — TLS traffic decryptable, digital signatures forgeable.
SENS-012.description: A PEM-encoded private key block (-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----) was detected in the API response. This is one of the most severe credential exposures — the private key can be used to decrypt TLS sessions, forge certificates, and impersonate the server.
SENS-012.solution: Revoke and rotate the exposed certificate/key pair immediately. Investigate how the private key reached the application database. Private keys must be stored only in HSMs or secrets managers.

SENS-013.label: Email Address Exposed in API Response
SENS-013.owasp: API3:2023 - Broken Object Property Level Authorization
SENS-013.impact: PII exposure — GDPR Article 5 violation, phishing and credential stuffing attack enablement.
SENS-013.description: Email addresses were detected in the API response. While email addresses are sometimes intentionally returned, their exposure in bulk or in endpoints accessible to unauthenticated users constitutes a GDPR-reportable PII leak and enables phishing campaigns and credential stuffing attacks.
SENS-013.solution: Apply the principle of data minimization — return email addresses only when strictly necessary and only to authorized users. Mask emails in list endpoints (e.g. j***@example.com).

SENS-014.label: Credit Card Number Exposed in Response (Luhn-Validated)
SENS-014.owasp: API3:2023 - Broken Object Property Level Authorization
SENS-014.impact: PCI-DSS violation — financial fraud, card cloning, regulatory penalties.
SENS-014.description: A credit card number passing Luhn validation was detected in the API response. PCI-DSS requires that Primary Account Numbers (PANs) be masked in all non-payment contexts. Storing or returning full card numbers is a severe compliance violation.
SENS-014.solution: Use payment tokenization. Never store or return full PANs. Return only masked representations (last 4 digits). Conduct a PCI-DSS compliance audit immediately.

SENS-015.label: Bearer Token Exposed in Response Body
SENS-015.owasp: API3:2023 - Broken Object Property Level Authorization
SENS-015.impact: Session hijacking — attacker can reuse the token to authenticate as the victim.
SENS-015.description: A Bearer token was detected in the API response body. Authentication tokens found in data responses indicate improper data isolation — tokens are being stored as application data and returned to API consumers, enabling token theft and session hijacking.
SENS-015.solution: Bearer tokens must only appear in authentication responses. Audit the data model to identify where tokens are stored as fields. Implement strict response serialization that excludes all credential fields.

SENS-016.label: Google API Key Exposed in Response
SENS-016.impact: Google Cloud service abuse — Maps, Gmail, Drive, and other APIs accessible at the account owner's expense.
SENS-016.description: A Google API key (AIza...) was detected in the API response. Depending on the key's permissions, an attacker can abuse Google Cloud services (Maps, Translation, Gmail, Drive) generating costs and potentially accessing private data.
SENS-016.solution: Rotate the key immediately in the Google Cloud Console. Restrict API keys to specific services and referrers/IPs. Never embed server-side API keys in client-facing API responses.

SENS-017.label: GitHub Personal Access Token Exposed in Response
SENS-017.impact: GitHub account and repository access — source code theft, supply chain attack via repository tampering.
SENS-017.description: A GitHub Personal Access Token (ghp_/gho_/ghu_/ghs_/ghr_) was detected in the API response. GitHub PATs grant access to repositories, organization membership, and depending on scope, can be used to push malicious code to production repositories.
SENS-017.solution: Revoke the token immediately on GitHub (Settings > Developer settings > Personal access tokens). Audit repository access logs. Use fine-grained tokens with minimal required scopes.
